about.title: about
about.paragraph_1: at the signals exhibition, interactive and passive-interactive* installations combine into a single statement about hopelessness and the frozen feeling that “it will always be this way.” one of the central themes is everyday fear and the inner control a person begins to exercise over themself. the installations respond to presence but never provide a complete answer, as if every initiative were cut off mid-sentence, leaving a sense that it is impossible to call out or express an opinion.
about.paragraph_2: we articulate all of this in our absurdly ironic manner. images are pushed towards the grotesque; individual works seem almost funny, but laughter quickly gives way to discomfort, and highly recognisable, painful situations emerge from behind the joke. irony becomes a way to speak about serious matters—about how difficult it is to inhabit an environment where everything suggests it is better to remain silent.

works.mirror: A mirror crossed by a metal grille hangs on the wall so that the viewer easily “steps into” its field of action without noticing. the installation is passive-interactive: the viewer does not actively interact with it, yet at some point catches their own gaze in the reflection and discovers themself on the other side of the work. one wrong step—and you find yourself “inside the zone” of its action.
works.fridges: three ordinary refrigerators stand in a row, each containing only one product: a bottle of vodka in the first, salt in the second, and a piece of dark bread in the third. this triad, familiar from a phrase in Pokrovsky Gates and from the soviet image of sufficiency, looks extremely modest and unsettling. the empty shelves turn “everything we need” into a question: are these symbolic goods truly enough to feel safe and prosperous, or are they merely a consoling gesture in conditions where nothing else is offered?
works.hammer_1: the work urges the viewer to become a participant in violence. the act of destruction does not disappear but immediately becomes a loop of repetition. a children’s toy originally designed to imitate laughter, voice, and play becomes a machine for recording and “reproducing” aggression.
works.hammer_2: what is usually perceived as a single gesture—a blow or an act of breaking—acquires duration and spreads through the space; the sound of the impact becomes the basis for the echo of mechanisms. importantly, the choice—whether to break or not—remains open, but the exhibition pushes towards action.
